chapter.title: The two bazaars and their price boards

cards.body:
The Sensex is just 30 shops out of thousands. So why does the whole country check it like the weather?

The bazaar has two big buildings, NSE and BSE. At each gate hangs a price board that sums up the biggest shops in one number. **One number for many shops** is handy, and it also hides a lot.
cards.simpler: The Sensex follows just 30 shops out of thousands. So why does the whole country check it like the weather? The bazaar has two big buildings, NSE and BSE. A price board hangs at each gate. It sums up the biggest shops in one number. **One number for many shops** is handy. But it also hides a lot.

cards.prompt: The evening news says: 'Nifty closed 0.8% down.' Your cousin Riya, halfway through a samosa, announces that all 50 companies lost money today. Is she right?

options.text: Yes. The board can only fall if every shop on it falls.
Not necessarily. Some shops could have gone up while the board still fell.
No. It means 0.8% of the 50 shops closed for the day.

whyNot.a: That treats the board like a vote everyone has to agree on, when it's really a summary: it's one combined number, so some shops can rise while it falls.
whyNot.c: That's counting shops, when it's really about prices: 0.8% is how much the combined price moved, not how many shops shut.

cards.reteach: A price board adds the 50 shops together into one number. If the big ones fall by more than the small ones rise, the total goes down. So a red board can still have plenty of green shops on it.

cards.title: Two buildings, two boards
cards.body:
The bazaar has two buildings: the *National Stock Exchange* (NSE) and the *Bombay Stock Exchange* (BSE). An *exchange* is just the place where buyers and sellers meet. Regular trading runs from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm, Monday to Friday. SEBI, the inspector, watches both.

**The Nifty 50 is NSE's board for 50 of its biggest shops. The Sensex is BSE's board for 30 of its biggest.** Each one is an *index*: a single number that tracks the combined price of its shops.

Walk into any bazaar and you see the big sign over the gate before you see a single stall. That's why the news reads out the board.
cards.simpler: The bazaar has two buildings: National Stock Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). An exchange is where buyers and sellers meet. Regular trading runs 9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays. SEBI, the inspector, watches both. **The Nifty 50 tracks 50 of NSE's biggest shops, and the Sensex tracks 30 of BSE's biggest.** Each is an index: one number for their combined price. Like the sign over a gate, it's seen first, so the news reads it out.

cards.title: A made-up board of three shops
cards.body: Take a made-up board with three shops: one giant worth ₹80 and two small ones worth ₹10 each, so ₹100 in total. Today the giant falls 2% and loses ₹1.60, while both small shops jump 5% and gain ₹1 between them. The board ends ₹0.60 lower, so it's **down 0.6%**. Two out of three shops had a great day, and the headline says the market fell.
cards.simpler: Picture a made-up board with three shops. One giant is worth ₹80. Two small ones are worth ₹10 each. That's ₹100 in total. Today the giant falls 2%, losing ₹1.60. Both small shops jump 5%, gaining ₹1 between them. The board ends ₹0.60 lower, so it's **down 0.6%**. Two of the three shops had a great day, yet the headline says the market fell.

cards.prompt: The Sensex is up 1% today. You own 1 share of a small paint company that isn't one of the Sensex 30. What do you actually know about your share?

options.text: It's up about 1%, same as the board.
Nothing yet. You'd have to look at its own price.
It probably fell, because money moved into the big 30.

whyNot.a: That's the board, not your shop: the Sensex only adds up its own 30 shops, and yours isn't one of them.
whyNot.c: That's a story, not a price: the board says nothing either way about shops that aren't on it.

cards.reteach: The Sensex is a summary of 30 named shops. A shop that isn't on the board isn't part of that total at all. To know how your shop did, read your shop's own price.

cards.title: Big shops shout louder
cards.body:
On both boards, **bigger shops count for more**. Size here roughly means the value of the company's shares that the public can actually trade, and a few giants take up most of the board. Picture one huge stall beside a row of tiny ones. When the huge stall has a bad day, it can drag the whole board down while dozens of small stalls quietly go up.

You'd think a board falling 0.8% means a typical shop fell 0.8%. It doesn't. It means the combined total fell 0.8%, with the giants counting most.

So the board tells you the mood at the big end of the bazaar. It doesn't tell you about any one shop, or about the thousands of shops that aren't on it.
cards.simpler: On both boards, **bigger shops count for more**. Size roughly means the value of the shares the public can trade, and a few giants fill most of the board. One huge stall's bad day can pull the board down while dozens of tiny stalls rise. A board down 0.8% doesn't mean a typical shop fell 0.8%. The combined total fell, with giants counting most. It shows the mood of the big shops, not any one shop or the thousands left off.

cards.body: At 2 pm Arjun sees 'Sensex tumbles' on his phone and panic-sells his one share in a pharma company. That evening he checks, and his pharma share had been up all day. He reacted to the board instead of his own shop. How to spot it: if a headline is pushing you to act, open your own share's price first.
cards.simpler: At 2 pm, Arjun sees 'Sensex tumbles' on his phone. In a panic, he sells his one share in a pharma company. That evening he checks, and his pharma share had been up all day. **He reacted to the board instead of his own shop.** Here's how to catch it: if a headline is pushing you to act, open your own share's price first.

cards.prompt: A friend asks you, 'So what is the Nifty 50, really?' Which answer is right?

options.text: The building where shares are bought and sold.
One number tracking the combined price of 50 of NSE's biggest companies, with bigger ones counting more.
The government body that keeps the shops honest.

whyNot.a: That's the exchange, not the board: NSE is the building, and the Nifty 50 is the board hanging at its gate.
whyNot.c: That's SEBI, the inspector, not the board: SEBI makes and enforces the rules, while the Nifty just reports prices.

cards.reteach: The bazaar has three things to keep apart: the building (NSE or BSE), the board at its gate (Nifty or Sensex) and the inspector (SEBI). The board is the only one that's a number. It adds up some of the biggest shops, and the giants count the most.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: NSE and BSE are the buildings; the Nifty 50 and Sensex are the boards at their gates, and the giants count most. **A board's move tells you the mood of the big shops, not how your own shop did.**
cards.simpler: NSE and BSE are the buildings. The Nifty 50 and Sensex are the boards at their gates, and the giants count most. **A board's move tells you the mood of the big shops, not how your own shop did.**

cards.body:
Look up the Nifty 50's last closing number on nseindia.com or any finance app you already have. Then open its list of gainers and losers (the shops that went up and down). On a down day, count how many still went up.

Tomorrow: your shares don't live with your broker. So where are they?
cards.simpler: Look up the Nifty 50's last closing number on nseindia.com or any finance app you already have. Then open its list of gainers and losers, meaning the shops that went up and the ones that went down. On a down day, **count how many shops still went up**. It's like checking each stall after hearing the bazaar had a bad day. Tomorrow: your shares don't live with your broker. So where are they?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now read 'Nifty closed 0.8% down' and say what it tells you about the 50 shops behind it, and what it doesn't.

dubious_claims: 'Size here means the total value of all a company's shares' is wrong as stated: the Nifty 50 and Sensex weight by free-float market cap, which counts only the shares available for public trading and leaves out promoter and locked-in holdings.

'NSE's board for its 50 biggest shops' and 'BSE's board for its 30 biggest' are simplified: membership also depends on free-float size, liquidity and sector balance, so the index is not strictly the 50 or 30 largest companies.
'Both open at 9:15 am' leaves out the 9:00–9:15 pre-open session. It's acceptable as a simplification, but it is not the full picture.
repairedFrom.why: The recap packs hours, both boards, share counts and weighting into one 50-word sentence that is hard to read on a phone, and its 'Tomorrow' hook is buried because the try card comes after it, so the chapter ends on a homework instruction instead.
repairedFrom.fix: Move 'Tomorrow: your shares don't live with your broker. So where are they?' to the very last line after the try card, and cut the recap's first sentence down to 'NSE and BSE are the buildings; the Nifty 50 and Sensex are the boards at their gates, and the giants count most.'
